title: Why Bell Curves Are Everywhere, and When They're Not

beats.text: A hundred waits for a bus: mostly short, with a long tail. [pause 0.15] Textbooks say the average of thirty is safe to treat as a bell. [pause 0.15] For these waits, does it take thirty, three hundred, or over a thousand? [pause 1.5]
A-B tests lean on that bell's tails, and on revenue data, thirty is off by a factor of thousands.
Maybe thirty just means collecting enough waits. [pause 0.15] Collect a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand. [pause 0.15] The bars get smoother, but the shape doesn't budge.

Measure the lean with skewness: the average cubed gap from the mean, left gaps counting negative, over the spread cubed. [pause 0.15] A perfect bell scores zero. [pause 0.15] These waits for a bus score about two at every sample size.
So average instead. [pause 0.5] Four bus waits: the one long wait gets diluted by three short ones. [pause 0.8] Drop that one number here. [pause 0.15] Do that ten thousand times.
These averages lean less: skewness one. [pause 0.15] Sixteen per average: point five. [pause 0.15] Sixty-four: point two five, nearly this perfect bell in green.
Each time the group grows four times, the skewness halves: two over root n, and two is the skewness of one wait.

The root comes from the cubes. [pause 0.15] Add four bus waits: their cubed gaps add up to four times one wait's. [pause 0.15] But the spread only doubles, so its cube grows eight times. [pause 0.15] Four over eight: half the lean. [pause 0.15] In general, n over n to the one and a half.

Kurtosis, the extra tail weight, fades faster: it quarters each time. [pause 0.15] Every finer difference fades faster still. [pause 0.15] Only the bell survives. [pause 0.15] That's the central limit theorem. [pause 0.15] It needs independent pieces, and one more condition.
Back to the textbook's thirty. [pause 0.5] Two over root thirty: point three seven. [pause 0.15] Close to a bell, by eye.

But tests live in the tails: a ninety-five percent interval should miss two and a half percent on each side. [pause 0.15] Tests estimate the spread from the same data. [pause 0.15] With lopsided waits, a low average comes with a small spread, so its interval stops short. [pause 0.8] With thirty waits: seven percent low, one percent high.

Ron Kohavi and colleagues want each side between two and three percent. [pause 0.15] Their rule: n at least three hundred fifty-five times the skewness squared. [pause 0.3] Divide by n and take the root: [pause 1.0] it's our formula: the average's skewness at most point oh five three. [pause 0.15] At three hundred, the lean is point one two: still too much. [pause 0.15] For these waits: fourteen twenty, lean point oh five three, and both misses reach the band. [pause 1.2]
Bing's revenue per user had a skewness near eighteen: a hundred and fourteen thousand users. [pause 0.15] Capping each user at ten dollars a week: under ten thousand.
And for some data, no number on this axis is enough.
A lighthouse one mile off a straight shore flashes at random angles, and each flash lands somewhere on the shore.
Track the average landing spot. [pause 0.15] It never settles: a flash aimed almost along the shore lands absurdly far away, and yanks it.

Among a thousand flashes, the farthest typically lands about nine hundred miles off. [pause 0.15] Divided by a thousand, it still drags the average about a mile. [pause 0.15] Half of single flashes land within a mile of the middle. [pause 0.15] Repeat the thousand-flash average two hundred times, and still only half do.
The theorem needs finite variance: no single piece can outweigh the rest. [pause 0.15] Here the variance is infinite. [pause 0.15] The median ignores how far the extremes fly, so it homes in.
So the answer is over a thousand, not thirty. [pause 0.15] Collect forever: still lopsided. [pause 0.15] The bell was never in the data. [pause 0.15] It's in the average.
